Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 112, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):

(Surat al-Ikhlas, the Sura of Sincerity). Four verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ Before delving into the tafsir, it is necessary to present several sections:

The first section: Ubayy narrated, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the sura ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ it is as if he has recited a third of the Qur'an, and he is given the reward of ten good deeds for each of those who associated partners with Allah and those who believed in Allah." The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him also said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ once, he is given a reward like that of one who believed in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, and he is given a reward like that of a hundred martyrs." It is also reported that Jibril (peace be upon him) was with the Messenger (peace be upon him) when Abu Dharr al-Ghifari approached. Jibril said: "This is Abu Dharr, who has approached." He (peace be upon him) said: "Do you know him?" He said: "He is more famous among us than he is among you." He (peace be upon him) said: "By what did he attain this virtue?" He said: "By his humility in himself and his frequent recitation of ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾." Anas narrated: "We were in Tabuk when the sun rose without its rays and light, and we had never seen it in that state before. All of us were amazed. Then Jibril descended and said: 'Allah has commanded that seventy thousand angels descend to pray over Mu'awiya ibn Mu'awiya. Would you like to pray over him?' Then he struck the earth with his wing, and the mountains were removed, and the Messenger (peace be upon him) appeared as if he were overlooking it, and he prayed over him, he and his companions. Then he said: 'Why did he attain what he attained?' Jibril said: 'He loved the sura of Sincerity.'" It is also reported: "He entered the mosque and heard a man supplicating and saying: 'I ask You, O Allah, O One, O Eternal Refuge, O He who begets not and was not begotten, and to whom none is equal.' He said: 'You are forgiven, you are forgiven, you are forgiven,' three times." And on the authority of Sahl ibn Sa'd: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and complained to him of poverty. He said: 'When you enter your house, greet whoever is in it, and if no one is in it, greet yourself, and recite ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ once.' The man did so, and Allah granted him provision abundantly, until he overflowed to his neighbours." And on the authority of Anas: "A man used to recite ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ in all his prayers."

The Prophet asked him about that, and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, I love it." He said: "Your love for it will admit you to Paradise." It has also been said: whoever recites it in a dream is given tawhid, few dependants, and frequent remembrance of Allah, and he is one whose supplication is answered.

The second section: concerning the cause of its revelation, and in it are several views:

The first: that it was revealed because of the question of the polytheists. Al-Dahhak said: "The polytheists sent Amir ibn al-Tufayl to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'You have split our ranks, reviled our gods, and opposed the religion of your fathers. If you are poor, we will enrich you; if you are mad, we will cure you; and if you desire a woman, we will marry you to her.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'I am not poor, nor mad, nor do I desire a woman. I am the Messenger of Allah, calling you from worshipping idols to worshipping Him.' They sent him again and said: 'Tell him to make clear to us the kind of your Lord: is He of gold or silver?' So Allah revealed this sura. They said to him: 'Three hundred and sixty idols do not meet our needs, so how can One meet the needs of all creation?' Then there was revealed: ﴿By those who range in ranks﴾ [al-Saffat: 1] up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, your God is One﴾ [al-Saffat: 4]. They sent him once more and said: 'Make clear to us His acts.' Then there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus: 3]."

The second: that it was revealed because of the question of the Jews. Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah, and with them was Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. They said: 'O Muhammad, this is Allah, who created creation; but who created Allah?' The Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him) became angry, and Jibril descended and calmed him, and said: 'Lower your wing, O Muhammad.' Then there was revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. When he recited it to them, they said: 'Describe for us your Lord: how is His upper arm, and how is His forearm?' He became angrier than his first anger. Then Jibril brought him the words: ﴿And they did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [al-An'am: 91]."

The third: that it was revealed because of the question of the Christians. 'Ata narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The delegation of Najran arrived and said: 'Describe for us your Lord: is He of emerald, or of ruby, or of gold, or of silver?' He said: 'My Lord is not of anything, for He is the Creator of things.' Then there was revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. They said: 'He is one, and you are one.' He said: 'There is nothing like Him.' They said: 'Give us more of a description.' He said: ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾. They said: 'And what is the Eternal Refuge?' He said: 'He to whom creatures turn in their needs.' They said: 'Give us more.' Then there was revealed: ﴿He neither begets, nor is He begotten﴾, as Mary bore, and ﴿nor is there to Him any equivalent﴾, meaning any counterpart from among His creation."

The third section: concerning its names. Know that the abundance of titles indicates greater excellence, and common usage bears witness to what we have mentioned. The first of them: the Sura of Isolation (al-Tafrid).

The second: the Sura of Stripping (al-Tajrid).

The third: the Sura of Divine Unity (al-Tawhid).

The fourth: the Sura of Sincerity (al-Ikhlas), because in this sura nothing is mentioned except His negative attributes, which are the attributes of majesty; and because whoever believes in it is sincere in the religion of Allah; and because whoever dies upon it, his deliverance is from the Fire; and because the sura before it was devoted to the condemnation of Abu Lahab, so the reward for whoever recites it is that he is not gathered together with Abu Lahab.

The fifth: the Sura of Salvation (al-Najat), because it saves you from likening Allah and from disbelief in this world, and from the Fire in the Hereafter.

The sixth: the Sura of Guardianship (al-Wilaya), because whoever recites it becomes one of the friends of Allah; and because whoever knows Allah in this manner has befriended Him. After a trial comes mercy, just as after a gift comes blessing.

The seventh: the Sura of Lineage (al-Nisba), because of what we have related, that it came as an answer to the question of one who said: "Trace for us the lineage of your Lord." And because he (peace be upon him) said to a man of Banu Sulaym: "O brother of Banu Sulaym, treat the lineage of Allah well." And this is one of the subtle expressions: when they said, "Trace for us your Lord's lineage," he said: "This is the lineage of Allah." Preserving lineages is a matter of the Arabs' custom, and they were strict with anyone who added to or subtracted from some lineages. So the lineage of Allah in this sura is more deserving of being preserved.

The eighth: the Sura of Knowledge (al-Ma'rifa), because the knowledge of Allah is not complete except by knowing this sura. Jabir narrated that a man prayed and recited ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "This is a servant who knows his Lord." Hence it was named the Sura of Knowledge for that reason.

The ninth: the Sura of Beauty. The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty." They asked him about that

and he said: "One, Eternal Refuge, who begets not and was not begotten." Because if He is One, without equal, it is permissible that such a likeness could take His place.

The tenth: the Sura of Dismissal (al-Muqashqisha). It is said: "The sick man was cured of his illness" (taqashqasha al-mariid mimma bihi). Whoever knows this is healed from polytheism and hypocrisy, because hypocrisy is a sickness, as He said: ﴿In their hearts is a sickness﴾ [al-Baqara: 10].

The eleventh: al-Mu'awwidha (the Protective Sura). It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) entered upon Uthman ibn Maz'un and sought refuge for him with it and with the two that follow it, then said: "Seek refuge with them, for you have never sought refuge with anything better than them."

The twelfth: the Sura of the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad), because it is specifically devoted to the mention of Him, exalted is He.

The thirteenth: the Sura of Foundation (al-Asas). The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "The seven heavens and the seven earths were founded upon ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾." Among what indicates this is that the claim of a Trinity is a cause of the ruin of the heavens and the earth, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿The heavens are about to burst apart from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse﴾ [Maryam: 90]. Therefore it is necessary that tawhid be the cause of the preservation of these things. It is also said that the reason for this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22].

The fourteenth: al-Mani'a (the Preventer). Ibn 'Abbas narrated that when he was taken up on the Night Journey, the Exalted said to His Prophet: "I have given you the Sura of Sincerity, and it is one of the treasures of the treasuries of My Throne; it is the Preventer, it prevents the punishment of the grave and the blasts of the fires."

The fifteenth: al-Mahdar (the Sura of Attendance), because the angels attend to listen to it when it is recited.

The sixteenth: al-Munaffira (the Repeller), because Satan flees at its recitation.

The seventeenth: al-Bara'a (the Sura of Immunity), because it is narrated that he (peace be upon him) saw a man reciting this sura and said: "As for this one, he has been freed from polytheism." And he (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever recites the sura ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ one hundred times, whether in prayer or otherwise, a written immunity from the Fire is granted to him."

The eighteenth: al-Mudhakkira (the Reminder), because it reminds the servant of pure tawhid. The recitation of the sura is like a brand-mark that reminds you of what you neglect and of what you need.

The nineteenth: al-Nur (the Light). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. He is the one who illuminates the heavens and the earth, and the sura illuminates your heart. He (peace be upon him) also said: "Indeed, everything has a light, and the light of the Qur'an is ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾." A parallel to this is that the light of a person is in his smallest organ, the pupil of the eye; so the sura is to the Qur'an what the pupil is to the human being.

The twentieth: al-Aman (the Security). He (peace be upon him) said: "When the servant says: There is no god but Allah, he enters My fortress, and whoever enters My fortress is safe from My punishment."

The fourth section: concerning its virtues, which are of several aspects:

The first: it is well known in the traditions that reciting this sura is equivalent to reciting a third of the Qur'an. Perhaps the purpose of this is that the highest aim of all the laws and acts of worship is knowledge of the essence of Allah, knowledge of His attributes, and knowledge of His acts; and this sura comprises knowledge of the essence. Therefore this sura is equivalent to a third of the Qur'an. As for the sura ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], it is equivalent to a quarter of the Qur'an, because the aim of the Qur'an is either action or abandonment, and each of these is either in the actions of the hearts or in the actions of the limbs, so the divisions are four. The sura ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ explains what should be abandoned among the actions of the hearts, so it in reality comprises a quarter of the Qur'an. For this reason the two suras, ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, share some names: they are the two Muqashqisha and the two Mubari'a, in that each of them conveys the heart's immunity from all besides Allah, exalted is He. Yet ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ by its wording conveys immunity from what is other than Allah and constant occupation with Allah, while ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ by its wording conveys occupation with Allah and constant turning away from other than Allah. Or, in that ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ conveys the heart's immunity from all objects of worship other than Allah, and ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ conveys the immunity of the object of worship from everything unbefitting to Him.

The second aspect: the Night of Power, because it was a truthful affirmation of the Qur'an, was better than a thousand months. The whole Qur'an is a shell, and the pearl is His saying: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. Therefore this sura obtained that excellence.

The third aspect: rational proof indicates that the highest rank of the servant is that his heart be illuminated by the light of Allah's majesty and greatness, and this is not attained except through this sura. Therefore this sura is the greatest of suras. If it is said: the attributes of Allah are also mentioned in the other suras, we reply: this sura has a distinctive property, namely that because of its brevity in form it remains preserved in hearts and known to minds, so the mention of Allah's majesty is ever present through it. Therefore it is distinguished from the other suras by these virtues. Now let us turn to the exegesis.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. In it are several issues:

**Question 1:** Know that knowing Allah, exalted is He, is a present paradise, for paradise is attaining what agrees with your intellect and your desire. That is why paradise was not a paradise for Adam when his intellect contended with his desire, nor was the grave a prison for the believer, because there he attained what suits his intellect and his desire. Moreover, knowing Allah, exalted is He, is something both desire and intellect want, so it becomes an absolute paradise. The explanation of what we have said is this: the intellect wants a trustworthy one with whom good deeds are deposited, while desire wants a wealthy one from whom pleasures are sought. Rather, the intellect is like a person of lofty aspiration who submits only to his Master, and desire is like a seeker of provision who, when he hears of the presence of a wealthy man, becomes eager to go to him. Furthermore, the intellect seeks knowledge of the Master so that it may thank Him for past blessings, while desire seeks it so that it may hope from Him for blessings yet to come. When they both knew Him as they wished, knowing and wealthy, they clung to the hem of His garment. The intellect said: "I will thank none but You," and desire said: "I will ask none but You." Then doubt came and said: "O intellect, how have you singled Him out for thanks, when perhaps He has an equal? And O desire, how have you limited yourself to Him, when perhaps there is another door here?" So the intellect remained bewildered, and that ease was disturbed for it. It wished to travel through the world of inference (istidlal) to win the pearl of certainty. Then it was as if the Truth, glorified is He, said: "How shall I disturb My servant's pleasure in occupying himself with My service and thanks?" So Allah sent His Messenger and said: "Do not say it from yourself; rather, say: He is the one you know to be truthful, who says to me: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾." Thus He made you know the oneness (wahdaniyyah) through revelation, and spared you the burden of reflection and inference through reason. The verification of this is that matters to be sought are of three kinds. One kind cannot be reached through revelation, and it is everything upon which the soundness of revelation depends, such as knowledge of the essence of Allah, exalted is He, His knowledge and His power, and the validity of miracles. A second kind cannot be reached except through revelation, and it is the occurrence of everything whose possibility of occurrence is known by reason. A third kind can be reached through both reason and revelation together, such as knowing that He is One and that He is not seen by eyes. We have fully explained the proofs of divine oneness in our commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾.

**Question 2:** Know that they agreed that Surat ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾ must include "Say" (qul). They also agreed that the word "Say" is not permitted in Surat (Tabbat) [Al-Masad]. As for this surah, they differed. The widely known reading is ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read it without "Say", thus: "He is Allah, the One." The Prophet ﷺ read it without "Say He," thus: "Allah is the One, Allah the Eternal Refuge." Whoever affirms "Say" says: the reason for it is to show that the composition is not within his power, but that he relates whatever is said to him. Whoever omits it says: so that it is not supposed that this was already known to the Prophet, peace be upon him.

**Question 3:** Know that there are several possibilities in the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this verse:
First: huwa is a pronoun referring to the name of Allah, so that "Allah" is raised as the predicate of a subject, and what may be said of "One" (ahad) is what may be said in your saying: "Zayd, your brother, is standing."
Second: huwa refers to the matter or the affair (al-sha'n), and on this interpretation "Allah" is raised as the subject, "One" is its predicate, and the clause is a predicate of huwa. The implied meaning is: the matter and the story is that Allah is One. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Then behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will be staring﴾ (Al-Anbiya: 97), except that "hiya" is in the feminine because the explanation contains a feminine noun. On this basis came: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded﴾ (Al-Hajj: 46). But when there is no feminine noun in the explanation, the pronoun of the matter is not made feminine, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ (Ta-Ha: 74).
Third: al-Zajjaj said: the implied meaning of this verse is: this which you asked about is "He is Allah, the One."

**Question 4:** Regarding "ahad" there are two views:
One of them: it has the same meaning as "wahid" (one). Al-Khalil said: it may be said, "ahad" is "ithnan" (two), and the original of "ahad" is "wahad," but the waw was changed into a hamza for ease. They usually do this with a waw that is vowelled with a damma or a kasra, as in their saying: wujuh and ujuh (faces), wisadah and isadah (cushion).
The second view: "wahid" and "ahad" are not synonymous names. Al-Azhari said: nothing is described by ahadiyyah (absolute oneness) except Allah, exalted is He. One does not say "rajul ahad" (a man, one) or "dirham ahad" (a dirham, one), as one says "rajul wahid" meaning single, alone with respect to something. Rather, "ahad" is an attribute of the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, which He has exclusively, so nothing shares it with Him. Then they mentioned several differences between "wahid" and "ahad":
First: "wahid" enters into "ahad," but "ahad" does not enter into "wahid."
Second: if you say, "No one can withstand so-and-so, except one," it is permissible to say, "But two can withstand him." Unlike "ahad": if you say, "No one can withstand so-and-so," it is not permissible to say, "But two can withstand him."
Third: "wahid" is used in affirmation, and "ahad" in negation. You say in affirmation, "I saw a man, one (wahid)," and in negation, "I did not see anyone (ahad)," which conveys generality.

**Question 5:** The readers differed regarding His saying: "ahadun Allahu al-samad." The common reading is with tanwin and its vowel is a kasra: "ahadun-ni Allahu" (with the nun sounded before the lam). This is the analogical form about which there is no difficulty, for the tanwin of "ahad" is silent and the lam of definiteness in "Allah" is silent. When two silent letters meet, the first of them is moved with a kasra. From Abu Amr: "ahadu Allahu," without tanwin. This is because the nun resembled the vowel letters (huruf al-lin) in that it is added as they are added, and when it resembled them, it was treated like them in being dropped when silent upon meeting another silent letter, just as the alif, waw and ya are dropped for this reason, as in: "ghazaa al-qawma" (he raided the people), "yaghzu al-qawma" (he raids the people), and "yarmi al-qawma" (he throws at the people). For this reason the silent nun is also dropped in the verb, as in: "lam yaku" (he was not) and ﴿So do not be in doubt﴾ (Hud: 109). Thus here it has been dropped in "ahadu Allahu" because of the meeting of two silent letters, just as these letters are dropped.
We have mentioned this in detail in our commentary on His saying: ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 30). It is also narrated from Abu Amr: "ahadu Allahi" (with the pause form). He said: I found the readers reading it this way in continuous recitation, with sukun. Abu Ali said: the word-final positions (fawasil) may take the same treatment in continuous speech as in pause. On this basis, those who said ﴿fa-adallūnā al-sabīla﴾ and ﴿rabbanā﴾ (Al-Ahzab: 67), and ﴿wa-mā adrāka mā hiyah﴾ and ﴿nār﴾ (Al-Qari'ah: 10), did so. Likewise, since most readers, as Abu Amr relates, read it in pause, he treated it in continuous speech as in pause, because the pause on it persists and is frequent on their tongues. Al-A'mash read: "Say: He is Allah, the One (al-wahid)." If it is asked: why? It is said: "ahad" is in the indefinite form. Al-Mawardi said: there are two views on this:
One of them: the definite article is omitted with the intention of supposing it, and the implied meaning is: "Say: He is Allah, the One (al-ahad)."
The second: the purpose is indefiniteness as a form of glorification.

**Question 6:** Know that His saying "huwa Allahu ahad" consists of three words, and each of them points to a station of the seekers:
The first station is the station of those brought near (al-muqarrabun), which is the highest of the stations of those travelling to Allah. These are the ones who looked at the quiddities (mahiyyat) and realities of things as they are in themselves. Therefore they saw no existent except Allah, because the Truth is the one whose existence is necessary in its essence, whereas everything else is possible in its essence, and what is possible in its essence, if considered in itself, is non-existent. These people saw no existent except the Truth, glorified is He. His saying "huwa" is an absolute indication, and although an indication is absolute, the thing indicated, being specific, makes that absolute restricted to that specific thing. Therefore our saying "huwa" was an indication, from these brought near, to the Truth, glorified is He. They did not need a distinguishing element in that indication, because the need for a distinguishing element arises only when two existents are present there, and we have shown that these people saw with the eyes of their intellects only the One alone. For this reason the word "huwa" was sufficient for these people to attain complete recognition.
The second station is the station of the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), which is below the first station. This is because they witnessed the Truth as existent and also witnessed creation as existent, so there arose a multiplicity in existents. Therefore "huwa" was not sufficient for indicating the Truth; there must be a distinguishing element by which the Truth is distinguished from creation. These people needed to join the word "Allah" to the word "huwa," so it was said for their sake: "huwa Allahu," because Allah is the existent upon whom everything else depends, and He is free of everything else.
The third station is the station of the companions of the left (ashab al-shimal), which is the lowest and most debased of the stations. These are the ones who allow that the Necessary Existent might be more than one, and that God might be more than one. Therefore the word "ahad" was joined with what preceded it, as a refutation of these people and a nullification of their statements. So it was said: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾.
Here there is another discussion, more noble and higher than what we have mentioned, which is this: the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, are either relational (idafiyyah) or negative (salbiyyah). The relational ones are like our saying: Knowing, Powerful, Willing, Creator. The negative ones are like our saying: He is not a body, nor a substance, nor an accident. Created things first indicate the first kind of attributes, and second, the second kind. Our saying "Allah" indicates the totality of the relational attributes, and our saying "ahad" indicates the totality of the negative attributes. Thus our saying "Allah is One" is complete in conveying the recognition that befits human intellects. We said that the word "Allah" indicates the totality of the relational attributes because Allah is the one who deserves worship, and deserving worship belongs only to the one who is independent in bringing things into existence and originating them. Independence in bringing into existence is attained only by one who is described by complete power, executing will, and knowledge related to all known things, both universals and particulars. These are the totality of the relational attributes. As for the totality of the negative attributes, these are absolute oneness (ahadiyyah), because what is meant by absolute oneness is that this reality is in itself single and free of all modes of composition. This is because every composite essence needs each of its parts, and each of its parts is other than it. Thus every composite is in need of something other than itself, and everything in need of something other than itself is contingent in its essence (mumkin li-dhatihi). Therefore every composite is contingent in its essence. The God who is the origin of all beings cannot be contingent; rather, He is in Himself single, one. When absolute oneness is established, He must not be spatially located (mutahayyiz), because every spatially located thing has a right side distinct from its left, and everything of this kind is divisible. So the one who is absolutely one is impossible to be spatially located, and if He is not spatially located, He is not in any place or direction. He must not be inherent in anything, for with His substrate He would not be one, and He must not be a substrate for anything, for with what inheres in Him He would not be one. If He is neither inherent nor a substrate, He is not changeable at all, because change must be from one attribute to another. Also, if He is one, He must be unique, for if two necessary existents were supposed, they would share necessity and differ in individuation, and what makes them share is other than what makes them differ, so each of them would be composite. Thus it is established that His being one entails His being unique. If it is asked: how can it be conceived that a thing is one? For every reality described by oneness, there is that reality, that oneness, and their combination; so that is a third of three, not one. The answer: oneness is a necessary property of that reality, so the thing judged to be one is that reality itself, not the aggregate formed from it and that oneness. Thus it has become clear, by what [has been said], [page 166]

We have mentioned that His saying, ﴿Allah is One﴾, is a statement that includes all of Allah's attributes, both the relational attributes and the negative attributes. The full discussion of this matter is found in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And your God is One God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163].

Concerning His words, ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad)﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: They have mentioned two interpretations of (al-Samad):

The first: It is a form (fa'al) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), from "samada ilayhi" (he turned to him/aimed at him) when he intended him, and it means the lord to whom one turns in needs. The poet said:

Has the messenger of death come early with the news of the best of the Banu Asad, of ʿAmr ibn Masʿud and of the lord al-Samad?

And he also said:

I struck him with my sword, then I said to him: "Take it, Hudhayf, for you are the lord al-Samad."

The evidence for the correctness of this interpretation is what Ibn ʿAbbas narrated: that when this verse was revealed, they said, "What is al-Samad?" The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "He is the lord to whom one turns in needs." Al-Layth said: "Samadtu samada hadha al-amr," meaning, "I aimed at the aim of this matter."

The second opinion: Al-Samad is the one who has no hollow (jawf). From this one says, "al-simad" for the stopper of a bottle, and "shay' musmad," meaning something solid without softness. Qatadah said: On this interpretation, the dal in it is a substitution for the ta', and it is al-musmat (the solid, impenetrable). Some of the later lexicographers said: al-Samad is the smooth stone that does not accept dust, nothing enters it and nothing comes out of it.

Know that some ignorant anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbihah) have used this verse as evidence that God, exalted is He, is a body. This is false, because we have shown that His being One (ahad) contradicts His being a body. So the premise of this verse indicates that it is impossible for al-Samad to mean this meaning. Moreover, al-Samad in this interpretation is a attribute of compressed bodies, and God is exalted above that. Therefore, it must be taken in its metaphorical sense, because a body of that kind is unaffected and unaltered by others, and this points to His being, glory be to Him, necessarily existent in His essence, incapable of change in His existence, His continuance and all His attributes. This is what relates to the linguistic discussion of this verse.

As for the exegetes, various views have been transmitted from them. Some of them fit the first interpretation, namely that He, exalted is He, is a lord to whom one returns for the removal of needs, and this points to the relational attributes (al-sifat al-idafiyyah). Others fit the second interpretation, namely that He, exalted is He, is necessarily existent in His essence and attributes, incapable of change in them, and this points to the negative attributes (al-sifat al-salbiyyah). Sometimes they explain al-Samad by something that combines both.

As for the first type, they have mentioned several views:

First: al-Samad is the All-Knowing of all that is known, because His being a lord to whom one returns for the fulfilment of needs is not complete except by that.

Second: al-Samad is the Forbearing (al-Halim), because His being a lord requires forbearance and generosity.

Third: This is the saying of Ibn Masʿud and al-Dahhak: al-Samad is the lord whose lordship has reached its completion.

Fourth: al-Asamm said: al-Samad is the Creator of things, because His being a lord requires that.

Fifth: al-Suddi said: al-Samad is the one aimed at in desires, the one sought for help in calamities.

Sixth: al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajali said: al-Samad is the one who does what He wills and judges what He desires; there is no one who can reverse His judgment, and no one who can repel His decree.

Seventh: He is the honoured, exalted lord.

Eighth: He is the unique, the glorious, whose matter is not decided without Him.

As for the second type, which points to the negative attributes, they have mentioned several views:

First: al-Samad is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), as He said: ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Hadid: 24].

Second: al-Samad is the one above whom there is no one, as He said: ﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18], and the one who fears no one above Him, and from whom no one below Him hopes; needs are raised to Him.

Third: Qatadah said: He does not eat or drink: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14].

Fourth: Qatadah said: He is the one who remains after the annihilation of His creation: ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman: 26].

Fifth: al-Hasan al-Basri said: He is the one who has always been and always will be, and to whom cessation cannot apply; He was without place, without where and without when, without throne or chair, neither jinn nor human, and He is now as He was.

Sixth: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: He is the one who does not die and is not inherited, and to Him belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth.

Seventh: Yaman and Abu Malik said: He is the one who does not sleep and does not forget.

Eighth: Ibn Kaysan said: He is the one who is not described by the attribute of anyone.

Ninth: Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: He is the one who has no defect.

Tenth: al-Rabi ibn Anas said: He is the one whom calamities do not befall.

Eleventh: Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: He is the one perfect in all His attributes and in all His acts.

Twelfth: Jaʿfar al-Sadiq said: He is the one who overcomes and is not overcome.

Thirteenth: Abu Hurayrah said: He is the one who is free of need from everyone.

Fourteenth: Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: He is the one whom creation has despaired of knowing the manner of.

Fifteenth: He is the one whom sight cannot perceive.

Sixteenth: Abu al-ʿAliyah and Muhammad al-Qurazi said: He is the one who did not beget and was not begotten, because everything will be inherited and everything born will surely die.

Seventeenth: Ibn ʿAbbas said: He is the Great, above whom there is no one.

Eighteenth: He is the one exalted above accepting deficiencies or excesses, above being the locus of changes and transformations, and above being encompassed by times, places, moments and directions.

As for the third way, which is to take the word al-Samad as encompassing all of these: this is possible, because according to its indication of necessary existence in itself, it indicates all the negations, and according to its indication of being the source of all things, it indicates all the divine attributes.

Second issue: His words, ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾, require that there be no samad in existence other than God. And if al-Samad is interpreted as the one to whom one turns in needs, or as that which does not accept change in its essence, it follows that there is no being of this kind in existence other than God, exalted is He.

So this verse indicates that there is no god except the One. His words, ﴿Allah is One (Ahad)﴾, indicate His unity, in the sense that there is no composition or combination in His essence in any way whatsoever. And His words, ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾, indicate His unity in the sense of negating partners, equals and opposites. Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: Why did "ahad" come indefinite while "al-samad" came definite? The answer: Most people's imaginations are dominated by the notion that every existent is perceptible, and it is established that everything perceptible is divisible. Therefore, what is not divisible does not occur to the minds of most people. As for al-Samad, it is the one to whom one turns in needs, and this was known to the Arabs, indeed to most people, as He said: ﴿And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87]. Since oneness (ahadiyyah) was unknown and strange to most people, while the samadiyyah was known and established to the majority, the word ahad came in indefinite form and the word al-samad in definite form.

Second question: What is the benefit of repeating the word "Allah" in His words, ﴿Allah is One (Ahad)﴾ and ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾? The answer: Had this word not been repeated, then both "ahad" and "samad" would have to appear either both indefinite or both definite, and we have shown that this is not permissible. Therefore the word was repeated so that "ahad" is mentioned indefinite and "samad" definite.

﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten.﴾ Concerning this verse, there are several questions.

**The first question:** Why is ﴿He neither begets﴾ placed before ﴿nor is He begotten﴾, when in the observable world a person is first begotten and then becomes a parent?

**The answer:** The start was made with "He does not beget" because they claimed that He has a son. The reason is that the polytheists of the Arabs said, "The angels are God's daughters." The Jews said, "Uzayr is the son of God." The Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of God." Nobody claimed that He has a parent. For this reason, He began with the more important point, saying ﴿He neither begets﴾. Then He pointed to the proof, saying ﴿nor is He begotten﴾. It is as if it were said: The evidence that sonship is impossible for Him is our agreement that He was not the son of anyone else.

**The second question:** Why did He restrict the statement to the past tense, saying ﴿He neither begets﴾ and not "He will never beget"?

**The answer:** He restricted it to this form because the verse came as a response to their saying, "God has begotten." The evidence for this is the verse ﴿Surely they say out of their lie: "God has begotten."﴾ [al-Saffat: 151]. Since the purpose of this verse is to refute their statement, and they made that statement in the past tense, the verse was revealed to match their words.

**The third question:** Why did He say here ﴿He neither begets﴾, while in the surah of Bani Isra'il He said ﴿nor has He taken a son﴾ [al-Isra': 111]?

**The answer:** Sonship (walad) can be of two kinds:

The first is that a being is begotten from him, one like himself. This is true sonship.

The second is that a being is not begotten from him, but he adopts it as a son and calls it by this name, even though it is not really his son. The Christians are of two groups. Some of them said, "Jesus is truly the son of God." Others said, "God took him as a son to honour him, just as He took Abraham as a friend (khalil) to honour him." So His saying ﴿He neither begets﴾ contains an indication of the negation of real parenthood. His saying ﴿nor has He taken a son﴾ indicates the negation of the second kind. For this reason, He said ﴿nor has He taken a son, nor has He any partner in dominion﴾, because a person may take a son in order that he may be a helper and assistant to him in an intended matter. Likewise, in another surah He said, ﴿They say: "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ [Yunus: 68]. This is an indication of what we have mentioned: that taking a son happens only when there is a need.

**The fourth question:** Can the negation of His being a parent and of His being begotten be known through revelation (sam')? If it cannot, what is the benefit of mentioning it here?

**The answer:** The negation of His being a parent is derived from knowing that He, exalted is He, is not a body, nor divisible into parts, nor separable into pieces. The negation of His being begotten is derived from knowing that He, exalted is He, is eternal (qadim). Knowledge of each of these two principles comes before knowledge of prophethood and the Qur'an. Therefore, these two cannot be derived from the revealed (sam'i) proofs. It remains to be asked: since these two are not derived from revelation, what is the benefit of mentioning them in this surah?

We say: We have already explained that what is meant by His being ONE (ahad) is that He, glory be to Him, in His essence and quiddity, is exalted above all modes of composition. His being the Self-Sufficient (samad) means that He is necessary in His essence (wajib li-dhatihi, that is, necessary existence through Himself), and that He cannot change in His essence or in all His attributes. Since this is so, oneness and self-sufficiency necessitate the negation of being a son and of being begotten. Since He mentioned the cause that necessitates the negation of being a parent and of being begotten, He therefore mentioned these two rulings. The purpose of mentioning them is for God, exalted is He, to alert us to the decisive rational proof for the negation of both.

**The fifth question:** Does God's saying ﴿He neither begets nor is He begotten﴾ have any benefit beyond the negation of sonship and the negation of being begotten?

**The answer:** It has many benefits. This is because His saying "God is One" (Allah ahad) points to His being, in His essence and quiddity, exalted above composition. His saying ﴿God, the Self-Sufficient﴾ points to the negation of opposites, equals, partners, and likenesses. These two lofty stations are ones on which there is agreement between the people of the religions and the philosophers. However, after this point, disagreement arose between the people of the religions and the philosophers. The philosophers said that from the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud) an intellect ('aql) is generated, and from that intellect another intellect, a soul, and a sphere are generated. Thus it continues in this order until it reaches the intellect that governs what lies beneath the sphere of the moon. According to this view, the Necessary Existent has begotten the first intellect that is below Him, and the intellect that governs this world of ours is like a being begotten from the intellects above it.

So the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted is He, first negated parenthood, as if it were said: He has not begotten the intellects and souls. Then He said: The being that governs your bodies, your spirits, and this world of yours is not begotten from anything else. So there is no parent, no begotten, and no originator except the One, who is the Truth, glory be to Him.

[Page 169]

**[Commentary of al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb, on Surah 112, verse 4]**

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him, anyone.﴾ On this verse there are two questions.

**The first question:** In eloquent Arabic, the adverbial complement (*al-zarf*) that is a non-fixed dependent (*lagh ghayr mustaqirr*) is placed after the thing it modifies, not before it. Sibawayh explicitly stated this in his book. So why does it occur in front in the most eloquent speech?

The answer: this statement was made only to deny equality to the Essence of God, and the word that expresses this meaning is this complement. Placing the more important element first is preferable, so for this reason the complement deserved to be placed first.

**The second question:** How is this verse recited?

The answer: it has been recited as *kufuwan* (كُفُوًا) with a damma on the *kaf* and the *fa*, and also with a damma or kasra on the *kaf* and a sukun on the *fa*. The original form is with the damma, and it was then lightened, like *tunub* and *tunb*, and *unuq* and *unq*. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said *kufw*, *kuf'* and *kifa'*, all with the same meaning, which is "equal" or "peer."

The exegetes have several opinions on it:

First, Ka'b and 'Ata' said: there is no equal to Him and no counterpart. From this comes *mukafa'a* (reciprocation) in recompense, because He gives a person something equal to what he has given.

Second, Mujahid said: He has no consort. As if the Exalted were saying: no one is a *kufu'* (suitable equal) for Him to marry. This is a rebuttal of those whom God reports as saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. So the explanation of this verse is like an emphasis on His saying: ﴿He begets not﴾.

Third, and this is the verified view: when He had explained that He is the One to whom one turns in fulfilling needs, and had excluded intermediaries from between Him and His creatures by saying ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾, as we have explained, He then concluded the surah by stating that none of the existent things can be equal to Him in any of the attributes of majesty and greatness. As for existence, there is no equality in it, because His existence is a necessary consequence of His reality, since His reality, considered in itself, is not susceptible to non-existence. As for all other realities, they are susceptible to non-existence. As for knowledge, there is no equality in it, because His knowledge is neither necessary (*darurI*), nor acquired through inference (*istidlali*), nor derived from the senses or from sight, and it is not subject to error or slip. The knowledge of created things is not like this. As for power, there is no equality in it; likewise mercy, generosity, justice, bounty and benevolence.

Know that this surah consists of four verses, and in its arrangement there are several kinds of benefits.

**The first benefit:** the beginning of the surah indicates that He, glory be to Him, is One, and the *Samad* indicates that He is Generous and Merciful, because one does not turn to someone as a *samad* unless he is a benefactor. ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾ indicates that He is absolutely self-sufficient and exalted above change, so He does not withhold anything at all, and His giving is not for the sake of bringing benefit or repelling harm, but purely out of benevolence. His saying ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾ is an indication of the negation of attributes that are not permissible for Him.

**The second benefit:** God, exalted is He, negated from His Essence kinds of multiplicity by His saying *Ahad* (One), negated deficiency and being overcome by the word *Samad*, negated being caused and being a cause by ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾, and negated opposites and rivals by His saying ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾.

**The third benefit:** His saying *Ahad* refutes the doctrine of the Dualists who believe in Light and Darkness, the Christians with their Trinity, and the Sabians with their belief in the spheres and stars. The second verse refutes the doctrine of whoever affirms a creator other than God, because if another creator existed, the Truth would not be the one to whom one turns for all needs. The third verse refutes the doctrine of the Jews regarding 'Uzair, the Christians regarding the Messiah, and the polytheists who claim the angels are daughters of God. The fourth verse refutes the doctrine of the polytheists who made idols equal to Him and partners with Him.

**The fourth benefit:** this surah, with regard to God, is like the surah of al-Kawthar with regard to the Messenger. But the reproach against the Messenger was on the basis that they said he was *abtar* (cut off), having no son. Here the reproach is on the basis that they attributed a son to God. The reason is that not having a son is a defect in a human being, while having a son is a defect with regard to God, exalted is He. For this reason He said here: (*Qul*, "Say") so that you may be defending me. And in the surah ﴿Indeed, We have granted you﴾, I say that statement so that I may be defending you. And God, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best.

[Page 171]

**(Introduction)**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Before plunging into the tafsir, two sections must be presented:

**The first section:** I heard that some of the knowers ('arifun) explained these two surahs in a wondrous manner. He said: when God, glory be to Him, explained the matter of divinity in Surah al-Ikhlas, He mentioned this surah right after it, in explaining the ranks of God's creatures. He said first: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ [al-Falaq: 1]. That is because the darkness of non-existence is infinite, and the Truth, glory be to Him, is the One who split those darknesses with the light of bringing into being, origination and innovation. Therefore He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, then He said: ﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾. The reasoning behind this is that the world of possibilities (*al-mumkinat*) is of two kinds: the world of command (*'alam al-amr*) and the world of creation (*'alam al-khalq*), as He said: ﴿Surely His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54].

The world of command is entirely pure goods, free from evils and calamities. As for the world of creation, which is the world of bodies and corporeal things, evil occurs only within it. The world of bodies and corporeal things is called the world of creation because *khalq* means measuring, and measure is one of the attributes of body. Since the matter is thus, it is inevitable that He said: "I seek refuge in the Lord who split the darknesses of the sea of non-existence with the light of bringing into being and origination, from the evils occurring in the world of creation, which is the world of bodies and corporeal things."

Then it is evident that bodies are either celestial (*athariyya*) or elemental (*'unsuriyya*). Celestial bodies are goods, because they are free from disorder and rifts, as He said: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Gracious no discrepancy. Look again: do you see any rift?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3]. As for elemental things, they are either inanimate (*jamad*), plant (*nabat*), or animal (*hayawan*). As for inanimate things, they are devoid of all psychic powers, so darkness in them is pure and light has wholly departed from them. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and from the evil of the darkness when it gathers﴾ [al-Falaq: 3]. As for plants, the vegetative power is that which increases in length, breadth and depth together. This vegetative power is as though it blows into the three knots. As for animals, the animal powers are the outer senses, the inner senses, appetite and anger, and all of these prevent the human soul from inclining toward the world of the unseen and occupying itself with the holy majesty of God. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾ [al-Falaq: 5].

Then, after this rank, nothing of the lower things remains except the human soul, and it is the one seeking refuge, so it cannot be something sought refuge from. Therefore He concluded this surah and mentioned after it, in the surah of al-Nas, the ranks and degrees of the human soul in its ascent. That is because by its original nature it is disposed to be imprinted with the knowledge of God, exalted is He, and love for Him, except that at the beginning it is entirely empty of these knowledges. Then, from the second rank, there come about primary, self-evident (*awwaliyya badihiyya*) sciences by which one can arrive at knowing unknown matters through reflection. Then, at the end of those unknown reflective matters, it passes from potentiality to actuality. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 1] is an indication of the first rank of the human soul, namely its state of being empty of all self-evident and acquired sciences. That is because in that rank the soul needs a trainer who trains it and adorns it with those self-evident knowledges. Then in the second rank, which is when these self-evident sciences are attained, it acquires a faculty for passing from them to seeking reflective sciences. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿King of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 2]. Then in the third rank, which is when those reflective sciences move from speech into action, the complete perfection of the soul is attained. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿God of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 3]. So it is as though the Truth names Himself according to each rank of the human soul by what befits that rank. Then He said: ﴿from the evil of the whisperer who withdraws﴾ [al-Nas: 4]. What is meant by it is the estimative faculty (*al-quwwa al-wahmiyya*). The reason for applying the name *al-khannas* (the one who withdraws) to the estimative faculty is that reason and the estimative faculty may agree in accepting some premises, but when the matter arrives at the conclusion, reason assists in the conclusion while the estimative faculty withdraws and refuses to accept the conclusion. For this reason the estimative faculty is called *al-khannas*. Then God, glory be to Him, explained that the harm of this *khannas* to reason is great, and that hardly anyone is free from it. So, as it were, God, glory be to Him, explained in this surah the ranks of human spirits, drew attention to their enemy, and pointed out what distinguishes reason from the estimative faculty. There is also the last rank of the degrees of the human soul, and therefore the Noble Book and the Great Criterion (*al-Furqan*) were concluded upon it.

**The second section:** They mentioned several reasons for the revelation of this surah:

First: "It is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said: Indeed an 'ifrit from among the jinn is plotting against you. He said: When you go to your bed, say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the two surahs."

Second: that God revealed them to him so that they would be a charm (*ruqya*) against the evil eye. It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that the Quraysh said: "Come, let us starve ourselves and cast the evil eye upon Muhammad." They did so, then they came to him and said: "How strong your arm is, how powerful your back is, and how radiant your face is!" So God revealed the two protecting surahs (*al-mu'awwidhatayn*).

Third, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes: "That Labid ibn A'sam, the Jew, bewitched the Prophet ﷺ with eleven knots, and tied them on a string, and cast them into a well called Dhi Arwan. The Messenger of God ﷺ fell ill, and this became severe for him for three nights. So the two protecting surahs were revealed for this, and Jibril informed him of the location of the sorcery. He sent 'Ali, peace be upon him, and Talha, and they came with it. Jibril said to the Prophet: Undo a knot and recite a verse. He did so, and every time he recited a verse, a knot came undone, until he found some relief and ease."

Know that the Mu'tazila denied all of this entirely. The Qadi said: "This narration is false. How is it possible to affirm its authenticity, when God says: ﴿and God will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 67], and He says: ﴿and the sorcerer does not prosper, wherever he comes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69]? Moreover, permitting it leads to a flaw in prophethood, because if it were true, it would be necessary that they could reach harm to all the prophets and righteous people, and they could have achieved great dominion for themselves. All of this is false. Also, the disbelievers used to reproach him by saying he is bewitched, so if this incident occurred, the disbelievers would have been truthful in that claim, and that defect would have been in him, peace be upon him. And it is well known that this is not permissible."

Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) said: "This story has been authenticated according to the majority of the people of transmission. The arguments mentioned have already been discussed under Surah al-Baqara. As for his saying that the disbelievers used to reproach the Messenger, peace be upon him, by calling him bewitched, and if this occurred the disbelievers would have been truthful in that saying, then his answer is this: the disbelievers meant by his being bewitched that he was insane, his intellect removed by means of sorcery, and therefore he abandoned their religion. As for his being bewitched with a pain he felt in his body, that is something no one denies. In sum, God did not allow anyone, neither a devil nor a human nor a jinn, to afflict him in his religion, his law and his prophethood. But as for harming his body, it is not far-fetched. The full discussion of this question has already been presented under Surah al-Baqara. Let us return to the tafsir."
